strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three diverse protein tasks (fitness, structure, function) with multiple models, datasets, and proper experimental methodology (validation sets, standard deviations, random seeds)
Clear practical motivation identifying genuine gap between general models optimized for average performance and practitioners' need for per-protein customization

Achieves state-of-the-art on ProteinGym benchmark and demonstrates improvements on challenging protein structures, with concrete visual examples (Figures 1, 3) showing dramatic improvements on individual targets
Provides useful analytical insight linking TTT to perplexity minimization with supporting correlation analysis (Figure 4), offering intuition for method effectiveness
Broad applicability demonstrated across diverse architectures (ESM2, SaProt, ESMFold, ESM3, TerpeneMiner, Light Attention) and task types (regression, classification, structure prediction)
Practical efficiency with 10 seconds for 50 TTT steps and commitment to reproducibility (code release, detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendix)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: TTT is established in computer vision (Gandelsman et al. 2022; Sun et al. 2020); application to proteins is straightforward adaptation without algorithmic innovation, representing incremental contribution marginal for top-tier venues

Modest improvements in headline results: ProteinGym primary benchmark shows only 0.3% improvement (SaProt 650M: 0.4569→0.4583); most improvements are 0.3-1.1%; validation performance often lags test performance (Table 6), suggesting potential overfitting

Shallow theoretical understanding: perplexity-minimization connection is partially circular; paper assumes correlation with downstream tasks implies causation without establishing mechanism or mechanistic insight into representation changes

Hyperparameter tuning requirement undermines 'no additional data' claim: number of TTT steps must be tuned on validation set; significant hyperparameter dependence (Figure 11) with poorly chosen settings hurting performance; reliance on task-specific confidence metrics (pLDDT)

Overfitting concerns with single-example fine-tuning: Figure 11 shows clear overfitting curve; validation results often lower than test results, raising concerns about test set overfitting despite perplexity/pLDDT-based early stopping

Unclear practical advantages: TraceptEVE achieves comparable ProteinGym results (0.4559 vs 0.4583) with one-time MSA computation; ESMFold+MP baseline competitive (0.4862 TM-score vs 0.5047 TTT on small 18-target set); cost-benefit analysis missing

Small evaluation sets for structure prediction (18 targets after filtering CAMEO); filtering by perplexity/pLDDT could introduce bias; no evaluation on proteins with rich evolutionary information to isolate TTT benefit beyond low-MSA regimes

Missing ablations: no study of masking strategy alternatives; inconsistent LoRA usage (ESMFold only); no layer-wise analysis or investigation of when/why TTT fails (Figure 9 shows degradation in some cases)

Statistical issues: improvements often within 1-2 standard deviations; no significance testing despite modest effect sizes; ESM2(650M)±0.00003 suggests extremely tight variance with minimal absolute change

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct protein prediction tasks (fitness, structure, function) with multiple models and datasets
Consistent empirical improvements across all tasks and metrics evaluated
Clear practical motivation addressing real needs of practitioners focused on individual proteins
Thorough experimental documentation with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Useful analysis of when TTT helps (low-MSA-depth proteins) and distribution of effects across test set
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward application of existing TTT methodology from CV to proteins without methodological innovation or technical contribution
Modest empirical improvements: fitness prediction ~0.3% improvement, function prediction 0.6-1% improvements; some results within statistical noise

Shallow theoretical justification: perplexity connection is circular (minimizing MLM loss directly minimizes perplexity); lacks principled explanation of why lower test perplexity improves downstream performance

Hyperparameter tuning undermines 'test-time' framing: requires validation-based tuning of TTT steps beforehand; high sensitivity to hyperparameters (Figure 11) limits practical applicability without external information
Overfitting concerns inadequately addressed: method relies on pLDDT (from the same model) to select steps; some proteins degrade (2/18 ESMFold, 1/18 ESM3) with minimal failure analysis
Questionable claims about distribution shift: paper claims benefits 'even without explicit distribution shift' but benefits primarily for challenging/atypical proteins, suggesting opposite conclusion
Limited baseline comparisons: no comparison to other test-time adaptation or augmentation methods; comparison to TraceptEVE/GEMME unfair since they use task-specific MSA information
Unsurprising insights: finding that TTT helps for low-MSA-depth proteins is expected; models naturally underperform on out-of-domain examples
Computational cost underexplored: ~20 second overhead per prediction not analyzed relative to modest improvements gained
Reproducibility concerns: despite promised code release, method requires substantial hyperparameter tuning for new settings with high variance in optimal parameters

strengths: Broad experimental validation: Comprehensive evaluation across three protein prediction tasks (fitness, structure, function) with six different models and multiple datasets demonstrates strong generality of the approach

Strong results on challenging cases: Particularly impressive improvements on proteins with low MSA depth and difficult structure prediction targets (e.g., TM-score improvements from 0.29 to 0.92), showing method targets right use cases
State-of-the-art fitness prediction: Achieves new benchmark record on ProteinGym (0.4583 for SaProt 650M, 40% improvement over previous leaderboard update), demonstrating competitive performance
Well-motivated and clearly presented: Clear articulation of why test-time adaptation matters for individual protein studies; Y-shaped architecture framing elegantly unifies disparate models

Practical design choices: Thoughtful engineering decisions (SGD optimizer selection, LoRA for large models, gradient accumulation) with good justification; pLDDT-based stopping criterion for structure prediction
Strong reproducibility: Commits to code release, comprehensive appendix with experimental details, hyperparameter grids (Table 4), new validation dataset (MaveDB with 676 assays)
Theoretical insight: Establishes connection between TTT and perplexity minimization with empirical validation (Figure 4: r=0.65-0.72 correlation for structure prediction)
Multiple seeds and standard deviations: Proper statistical reporting across five random seeds with consistent results indicates robustness
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core TTT method adapted from existing computer vision work (Sun et al. 2020; Gandelsman et al. 2022); contribution is primarily domain application rather than methodological innovation

Hyperparameter tuning requirement contradicts core claim: Method requires validation data to tune learning rate, batch size, TTT steps, and LoRA rank (Table 4); undermines 'without additional data' framing, and Figure 11 shows significant sensitivity (~0.007 Spearman range)

Modest absolute improvements in key scenarios: Fitness prediction shows small gains (ESM2 35M: +0.0196 Spearman, 6% relative; SaProt 650M MaveDB: 0.4926→0.4926 no improvement); function prediction improvements 0.6-1% (TPS mAP, localization accuracy)
Insufficient failure mode analysis: Figure 9 shows TTT degrades 2/18 ESMFold and 1/18 ESM3 cases; no investigation into success vs. failure conditions; unclear when practitioners should NOT use TTT

Limited sample sizes and potential selection bias: Structure evaluation uses only 18/194 CAMEO targets (filtered to challenging); fitness validation uses 50/483 proteins; subsets may not be representative

Incomplete mechanism explanation: Perplexity connection (Section 3.3) is correlational; unclear why minimizing pseudo-perplexity on single test example should improve downstream tasks with different training objectives

Computational cost inadequately characterized: ESM3 overhead ~20 seconds per protein (Figure 7) but no total pipeline cost analysis; impracticality for large-scale applications not discussed; computational burden vs. MSA approaches not compared

Weak alternative baselines: ESMFold + MP (masked prediction) is relatively weak baseline; limited comparison to other test-time adaptation methods from vision/NLP literature; no comparison to MSA-based adaptation despite dismissing it

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across three major tasks (structure, fitness, function prediction), multiple models (ESMFold, ESM3, HelixFold-Single), and multiple datasets (CAMEO, ProteGym, BFVD, MaveDB)
Addresses a genuine practical problem in computational biology with a simple, intuitive solution that is easy to integrate into existing pipelines

Consistent improvements across diverse experimental conditions (different model architectures, sizes, and masking strategies), with particularly strong results on challenging/out-of-distribution cases (19% improvement on BFVD viral proteins)
Excellent reproducibility with open-source PyTorch implementation, detailed hyperparameters in appendices, and computational efficiency (single GPU, 30-120 seconds per protein)
Clear and well-organized presentation with informative figures, honest discussion of limitations, and thorough experimental details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution applies standard masked language modeling at test time, which is a known technique from other domains; the innovation is primarily in application rather than methodology

Weak theoretical justification for why minimizing language model perplexity on a single protein sequence should improve structure/function prediction; the mechanistic explanation is circular and lacks principled grounding

Insufficient mechanistic understanding of what the model learns: the paper demonstrates that customization helps but provides limited analysis of which representations are modified, how they change, or why these changes improve downstream tasks

Incomplete failure mode analysis with important limitations relegated to appendix: limited discussion of when/why the method fails (Figure A6), what protein properties predict failure, or how common negative cases are in practice
Modest improvements in some settings, particularly fitness prediction (0.01-0.02 Spearman correlation gains in Table 2), with limited statistical significance testing and some overlapping error bars

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: different models require different numbers of steps (30 vs 50), and the pLDDT-based stopping criterion is heuristic; comprehensive hyperparameter search (Figures A10-A11) is relegated to appendix

Incomplete evaluation of practical utility: function prediction results are in appendix despite being a critical application; case studies are compelling but cherry-picked examples; computational cost-benefit trade-off (30-120 seconds per protein) deserves more analysis

Limited baseline comparisons: most comparisons are against base models rather than other domain adaptation or test-time training methods; alternative approaches to single-protein customization are not explored

MSA treatment feels incomplete: while important for real applications, the extension to multiple sequence alignments (Appendix B) receives minimal discussion; unclear whether practitioners should use MSA or single-sequence version and why

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three downstream tasks (structure, fitness, function prediction) and multiple pre-trained models with extensive benchmarks
Clear demonstration of effectiveness on challenging out-of-distribution cases, particularly 19% improvement on Big Fantastic Virus Database where general models struggle
Practical implementation with code provided, making the method accessible and reproducible
Extensive supplementary material with detailed experimental protocols, hyperparameters, and ablation studies
Well-organized presentation with clear experimental setup and multiple evaluation metrics
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward application of existing techniques (test-time training + masked language modeling) without methodological or theoretical innovation
Marginal and inconsistent improvements: typical gains of 0.09-0.5 with large standard deviations; many results fall within error margins without proper statistical significance testing
Severe computational overhead (60× cost compared to base models), which fundamentally undermines practical applicability and contradicts the utility narrative

Hyperparameter sensitivity requiring careful tuning of multiple parameters (learning rate, gradient accumulation, masking strategy, number of steps) with circular validation criteria based on model confidence

Lack of theoretical justification for why fine-tuning on a single target sequence should improve generalization; raises questions about whether the method is learning generalizable patterns or overfitting to task-specific details
Overfitting risk from fine-tuning on single sequences with no validation set; no principled method for selecting hyperparameters without ground truth
Weak baseline comparisons; missing comparisons to other test-time adaptation and domain adaptation methods
High risk of statistical artifacts: no formal significance testing, no correction for multiple comparisons, and improvements often within reported error bars
Limited problem relevance: substantial improvements occur only on rare out-of-distribution cases; most in-distribution proteins show minimal gains
Questionable experimental design: small CAMEO test set (45 proteins), newly constructed MaveDB with unvalidated quality, and highly variable results across tasks

strengths: Novel application of test-time training to protein machine learning, addressing an important gap between broad optimization and individual protein precision

Exceptionally thorough experimental evaluation across three downstream tasks (structure, fitness, function) with multiple models (ESMFold, HelixFold, ESM3), scales (35M-1.4B parameters), and datasets (CAMEO, ProteinGym, MaveDB, BFVD)

Consistent improvements demonstrated across all evaluated configurations with particularly impressive results on challenging targets (19% improvement on BFVD viral proteins, 60% of antibody CDRs improved)
Strong emphasis on reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, PyTorch package release, and clear integration examples
Practical utility demonstrated through compelling case studies and computational efficiency (faster than AlphaFold2 while maintaining competitive performance)
Formal theoretical justification provided in Appendix A linking test-time customization to perplexity minimization
Rigorous experimental methodology with multiple random seeds, error bars, statistical testing, and appropriate task-specific metrics

Shallow theoretical understanding of why perplexity minimization on a single sequence improves downstream performance; mechanistic insights are limited

Hyperparameter complexity undermines practicality - different models and tasks require different hyperparameters (Table A3), requiring practitioners to perform grid searches despite claims of efficiency
Incomplete baseline comparisons - missing comparisons with other test-time adaptation methods and simpler alternatives like fine-tuning only downstream heads

Limited failure analysis and generalization study - Figure A6 shows failures with minimal explanation; all experiments use in-distribution sequences; no evaluation on out-of-distribution proteins
